questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
{n}^{3}-1\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is

$$
n\text{ is not odd}\,⇒\,{n}^{3}-1\text{ is not even}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,{n}^{3}-1\text{ is odd}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is $\text{even},$ then
$n=2a,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{3}-1$ and show it is odd by writing it as  one more than a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{3}-1,$ we can show that ${n}^{3}-1=2b+1,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since ${n}^{3}-1$ $\text{is one more than}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that ${n}^{3}-1$ is $\text{odd}.$

Let $n$ be an integer. Then $2{n}^{2}-7n+1$ is odd only if $n$ is even.

A proof schema is outlined below. Fill in the missing entries.

The contrapositive form of the statement is as follows:

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
2{n}^{2}-7n+1\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,n\text{ is even}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is

$$
n\text{ is not even}\,⇒\,2{n}^{2}-7n+1\text{ is not odd}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,2{n}^{2}-7n+1\text{ is even}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

If $n$ is $\text{odd},$ then
$n=2a+1,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into the expression $2{n}^{2}-7n+1$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a+1$ into the expression $2{n}^{2}-7n+1,$ we can show that $2{n}^{2}-7n+1=2b,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since $2{n}^{2}-7n+1$ $\text{is}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that $2{n}^{2}-7n+1$ is $\text{even}.$

Let $n$ be an integer. If ${n}^{2}-2n$ is odd, then $n$ is odd.

The contrapositive form of the statement is as follows:

$$

If $n$ is {{field-3}}, then $n=$ {{field-4}}, where $a$ is {{field-5}}.

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
{n}^{2}-2n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is

$$
n\text{ is not odd}\,⇒\,{n}^{2}-2n\text{ is not odd}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,{n}^{2}-2n\text{ is even}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is $\text{even},$ then
$n=2a,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{2}-2n$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{2}-2n,$ we can show that ${n}^{2}-n=2b,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since ${n}^{2}-2n$ $\text{is}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that ${n}^{2}-2n$ is $\text{even}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
5n+4\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is even}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is not even}\,⇒\,5n+4\text{ is not even}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,5n+4\text{ is odd}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

If $n$ is $\text{odd},$ then
$n=2a+1,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into the expression $5n+4$ and show it is odd by writing it as one more than a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a+1$ into the expression $5n+4,$ we can show that $5n+4=2b+1,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since $5n+4$ $\text{is one more than}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that $5n+4$ is $\text{odd}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
3n-8\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is even}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is not even}\,⇒\,3n-8\text{ is not even}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,3n-8\text{ is odd}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

If $n$ is $\text{odd},$ then
$n=2a+1,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into the expression $3n-8$ and show it is odd by writing it as one more than a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a+1$ into the expression $3n-8,$ we can show that $3n-8=2b+1,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since $3n-8$ $\text{is one more than}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that $3n-8$ is $\text{odd}.$

Let n be an integer. Then n is even whenever 3n−8 is even.

A proof schema is outlined below. Fill in the missing entries.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

n is odd

3n−8 is even
n is even

3n−8 is odd
3n−8 is odd
n is odd
3n−8 is even
n is even
{(n is odd)(S0)}⇒{(3n−8 is odd)(S1)}

If n is
odd
odd
even
, then n=
2a+1
2a+1
2a
, where a is
an integer
an integer
a natural number
positive
negative

Substituting
n=2a+1
n=2a+1
n=2a
into the expression 3n−8, we can show that 3n−8=
2b+1
2b+1
2b
, where b is
an integer
an integer
a natural number
positive
negative
.

is one more than

is
a multiple of 2, we conclude that 3n−8 is

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
{{field-1}}\,⇒\,{{field-2}}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

If $n$ is {{field-3}}, then $n=$ {{field-4}} for some integer $a.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}7n+6 & ={{field-5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=$ {{field-6}}. Since $a$ is {{field-7}}, we have that $b$ is {{field-8}}.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7n+6 & ={{field-9}}\end{aligned}
$$

which {{field-10}} a multiple of $2.$ Hence, $7n+6$ is {{field-11}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
7n+6\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,7n+6\text{ is even}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression $7n+6$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of  $2$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}7n+6 & =7(2a)+6 \\  & =14a+6 \\  & =2{{(7a+3)}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=7a+3$ (highlighted above), we have that $7n+6=2b,$ which shows that $7n+6$ is indeed  a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=7a+3.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7n+6 & =2{{(7a+3)}_{⏟}}_{b} \\  & =2b,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, $7n+6$ is even.

Let $n$ be an integer. Using the contrapositive, prove that $3n+8$ is odd implies $n$ is odd.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
{{field-1}}\,⇒\,{{field-2}}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

If $n$ is {{field-3}}, then $n=$ {{field-4}} for some integer $a.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+8 & ={{field-5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=$ {{field-6}}. Since $a$ is {{field-7}}, we have that $b$ is {{field-8}}.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+8 & ={{field-9}}\end{aligned}
$$

which {{field-10}} a multiple of $2.$ Hence, $3n+8$ is {{field-11}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
3n+8\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,3n+8\text{ is even}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression $3n+8$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of  $2$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+8 & =3(2a)+8 \\  & =6a+8 \\  & =2{{(3a+4)}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=3a+4$ (highlighted above), we have that $3n+8=2b,$ which shows that $3n+8$ is indeed  a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=3a+4.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+8 & =2{{(3a+4)}_{⏟}}_{b} \\  & =2b,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, $3n+8$ is even.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
{{field-1}}\,⇒\,{{field-2}}
$$

We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

If $n$ is {{field-3}}, then $n=$ {{field-4}} for some integer $a.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{3} & ={{field-5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=$ {{field-6}}. Since $a$ is {{field-7}}, we have that $b$ is {{field-8}}.

Therefore, we have

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
{n}^{3}\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is even}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,{n}^{3}\text{ is odd}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

If $n$ is odd, then $n=2a+1$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into the expression ${n}^{3}$ and show it is odd by writing it as a multiple of $2,$ plus $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{3} & =(2a+1)^{3} \\  & =8{a}^{3}+12{a}^{2}+6a+1 \\  & =(8{a}^{3}+12{a}^{2}+6a)+1 \\  & =2{{(4{a}^{3}+6{a}^{2}+3a)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=4{a}^{3}+6{a}^{2}+3a$ (highlighted above), we have that ${n}^{3}=2b+1,$ which shows that ${n}^{3}$ is indeed one more than a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=4{a}^{3}+6{a}^{2}+3a.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{3} & =2{{(4{a}^{3}+6{a}^{2}+3a)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1 \\  & =2b+1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is one larger than a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, ${n}^{3}$ is odd.

Let $n$ be an integer. Prove that $n$ is odd provided that ${n}^{2}-5n+5$ is even.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
{{field-1}}\,⇒\,{{field-2}}
$$

We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

If $n$ is {{field-3}}, then $n=$ {{field-4}} for some integer $a.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-5n+5 & ={{field-5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=$ {{field-6}}. Since $a$ is {{field-7}}, we have that $b$ is {{field-8}}.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-5n+5 & ={{field-9}}\end{aligned}
$$

which {{field-10}} a multiple of $2.$ Therefore ${n}^{2}-5n+5$ is {{field-11}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
{n}^{2}-5n+5\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,{n}^{2}-5n+5\text{ is odd}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{2}-5n+5$ and show it is odd by writing it as a multiple of $2,$ plus $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-5n+5 & =(2a)^{2}-5(2a)+5 \\  & =4{a}^{2}-10a+5 \\  & =(4{a}^{2}-10a+4)+1 \\  & =2{{(2{a}^{2}-5a+2)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=2{a}^{2}-5a+2$ (highlighted above), we have that ${n}^{2}-5n+5=2b+1,$ which shows that ${n}^{2}-5n+5$ is indeed one more than a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=2{a}^{2}-5a+2.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-5n+5 & =2{{(2{a}^{2}-5a+2)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1 \\  & =2b+1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is one larger than a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, ${n}^{2}-5n+5$ is odd.

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose we wish to construct a proof by contrapositive of the following statement:

Let $n$ be an integer. Then $4n^2+5n-1$ is odd only if $n$ is even.

What are the missing entries in the proof template below?

The contrapositive form of the statement is as follows:

$$
\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{vvvxxxyyyzzz} } {\phantom{}} \, 
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{vvvxxxyyyzzz} } {\phantom{}} \,
$$

If $n$ is $\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }$ , then $n=\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }$, where $a$ is $\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{vvvxxxyyyzzz} }.$

Substituting $\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }$ into the expression $4n^2+5n-1,$ we can show that 

$$
4n^2+5n-1 = \bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }, \text{ where } b \text{ is } \bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }.
$$

Therefore, since $4n^2+5n-1$ $\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that $4n^2+5n-1$ is $\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{xxxyyy} }$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
4n^2+5n-1 \text{ is odd}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
n \text{ is even}
$$

To prove $P \Rightarrow Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is

$$
n \text{ is not even}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
4n^2+5n-1 \text{ is not odd}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}n \text{ is odd}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4n^2+5n-1 \text{ is even}}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

If $n$ is $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{odd}},$ then
$n = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2a+1},$
where $a$ is $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{an integer}}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into the expression $4n^2+5n-1$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of $2.$

Substituting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14274149/assets/bf27c298a76aa723be9bb5e4d334166aed9b1a556fc9e3e806d01d1545600ace.svg) into the expression $4n^2+5n-1,$ we can show that $4n^2+5n-1 = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2b},$ where $b$ is $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{an integer}}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since $4n^2+5n-1$ $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{is}}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that $4n^2+5n-1$ is $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{even}}.$

Example: 
                    Proving the Parity of a Linear Expression
canonical_examples.problem: Let $n$ be an integer. Using the contrapositive, prove that $n$ is odd whenever $3n-1$ is even.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
3n-1 \text{ is even}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
n \text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P \Rightarrow Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n \text{ is even}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
3n-1 \text{ is odd}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression $3n-1$ and show it is odd by writing it as a multiple of $2,$ plus $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3n-1 & =3(2a)-1 \\  & =6a-1 \\  & =(6a-2)+1 \\  & =2{{(3a-1)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=3a-1$ (highlighted above), we have that $3n-1 = 2b+1,$ which shows that $3n-1$ is indeed one more than a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=3a-1.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3n-1 & =2{{(3a-1)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1 \\  & =2b+1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is one larger than a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, $3n-1$ is odd.

                    Proving the Parity of a Nonlinear Expression
canonical_examples.problem: Let $n$ be an integer. Prove that $n^3 + 1$ is even only if $n$ is odd.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $a$ such that $n = 2a.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $a$ such that $n = 2a+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
n^3 + 1 \text{ is even} \quad\Rightarrow\quad n \text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P \Rightarrow Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
n \text{ is even} \quad\Rightarrow\quad n^3 + 1 \text{ is odd}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is even, then $n = 2a$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n = 2a$ into the expression $n^3 + 1$ and show it is odd by writing it as a multiple of $2,$ plus $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{3}+1 & =(2a)^{3}+1 \\  & =8{a}^{3}+1 \\  & =2{{(4{a}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{b}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b = 4a^3$ (highlighted above), we have that $n^3+1 = 2b+1,$ which shows that $n^3+1$ is indeed one more than a multiple of $2.$

Let $b = 4a^3.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{3}+1 & =2{{(4{a}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{b}+1 \\  & =2b+1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is one larger than a multiple of $2.$

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, $n^3+1$ is odd.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
One type of **indirect proof** is the so-called **proof by contrapositive.** The method is based on the fact that the implication 

$$
P \Rightarrow Q
$$

is logically equivalent to its contrapositive 

$$
\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P.
$$

So, instead of proving the statement directly, we can instead prove its contrapositive form. 

The outline of a typical contrapositive proof is the following:

**Statement.** *If $P,$ then $Q.$* 

*Proof.* 

Since $P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P,$ we'll prove the contrapositive $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P.$

**Assumption:** *Suppose $\lnot Q.$*

*Explanation of what $\lnot Q$ means using axioms, definitions, or other results.*

*Algebraic techniques, logic, and further definitions or axioms are used to demonstrate, through a series of inferences, that $\lnot Q$ implies $\lnot P.$* 

**Conclusion:** *Therefore, $\lnot P.$* So, since $\lnot Q\Rightarrow \lnot P,$ by the contrapositive $P\Rightarrow Q.$

In many cases, proving the contrapositive form of a statement is easier than proving the original statement. In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove parity statements using the contrapositive.

tutorials.name: Proving Parity Statements by Contrapositive
tutorials.problem:
Let's prove the following proposition using the contrapositive: 

$$
\underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is odd}}_{P(n)}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{n \text{ is odd}}_{Q(n)}
$$

To prove $P \Rightarrow Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.$ So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

*The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:*

$$
\underbrace{ n \text{ is even}}_{\lnot Q(n)}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is even}}_{\lnot P(n)}
$$

We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

*If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$*

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression $3n+2$ and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of $2.$

*Therefore,*

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+2 & =3(2a)+2 \\  & =6a+2 \\  & =2{{(3a+1)}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=3a+1$ (highlighted above), we have that $3n+2 = 2b,$ which shows that $3n+2$ is indeed  a multiple of $2.$

*Let $b=3a+1.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.*

*Hence, we have*

$$
\begin{aligned}3n+2 & =2{{(3a+1)}_{⏟}}_{b} \\  & =2b,\end{aligned}
$$

*which is a multiple of $2.$*

Finally, we write our conclusion.

*Therefore, $3n+2$ is even. *

Now that we've figured out the details, let's state the full proof.
